OpenAI Just Gave Its Agents a Wallet. Musk Says the Agent Flood Is Coming.

Your agent can now pay. For now, it still has to ask you first.

On Friday, Nov. 13, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet. It lets "dots," the company's always-on agents, finish a checkout for you with a saved credit card.

The pitch fits in one line from OpenAI's launch post: "It’s the first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase."

The product is narrow. The question behind it is not: once software holds the card, who sets the limits, who earns the fee, and what changes when the human tap goes away?

What OpenAI actually shipped
Wallet was built in partnership with American Express, Mastercard and Visa. It lives inside dots and nowhere else. OpenAI's help page says plainly: "Wallet isn’t available in Chat, Work, or standalone Codex threads."

The first wave is small on purpose:

ChatGPT Pro subscribers only
18 or older, living in the US, with a US billing address
Eligible US-issued American Express, Chase, Mastercard and Visa cards
Chase is not in the launch post's partner line, but the help page lists its cards as eligible, with a catch: "To add an eligible Chase card, you must be the primary cardholder, not an authorized user."

Also easy to miss: "ChatGPT Wallet doesn’t support debit cards." And the rollout is gradual, so even eligible users may not see it yet.

How a purchase works
You add a card once in a secure form, not in chat. Then you ask your dot to shop.

At checkout, the dot stops and asks. You review the merchant, items, total and card. Then you approve with biometrics: Face ID or Touch ID on a supported device, in the help page's words; "Face ID or a fingerprint scan" in the launch post.

OpenAI says that approval "creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make."

Only then does money move. The payment network issues a payment token, which OpenAI calls "a substitute for the user’s actual card details," complete with its own card number, security code and expiration date. The charge lands on your real card. The agent and the merchant never see the real number.

The Verge compared it to tap to pay and Apple Pay.

One detail in the help page is worth reading twice. "Ready to check out" means your approval is complete. "It does not confirm that the merchant has placed your order." Your approval and the store's order are two different events.

Who holds what
OpenAI's Wallet terms spell out the roles.

The merchant is the seller. The terms say: "The merchant is the seller and merchant of record." Returns, refunds and cancellations go to the store.

Your bank still decides. The issuer authorizes the charge, and your cardholder agreement, including rewards and dispute rights, still applies.

OpenAI sits in the middle. It stores the card and runs the approval. But the terms say OpenAI "does not decide or fund merchant refunds or card chargebacks unless required by law or OpenAI separately promises otherwise."

The wallet is OpenAI's, the account is your bank's, the sale is the store's.

Who takes the fee?
This is the part with the least on the record.

CNBC reported that Wallet could eventually open a new revenue stream for OpenAI, but that the company said it is not taking a cut of transactions to start.

That is all we found. OpenAI's launch post and help page describe no fee to users or merchants, and no source we checked compares card-network fees here with ordinary online checkout.

What OpenAI did say is where its attention is. "Our goal here is to really focus on merchants and our network partners and start building out a really great foundation that's safe and easy to use," Chaya Nayak, who leads product for monetization and payments at OpenAI, told CNBC.

Whether OpenAI ever charges, and whom, is open.

The store has to let the agent in
OpenAI is blunt about this. To accept Wallet, "websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents."

Its business guidance warns that fraud systems "may still flag legitimate purchases made by agents, leading to declines or cancellations." OpenAI says it is working with fraud-prevention firms and payment processors, including Stripe and Adyen, on that.

Not every store wants in. CNBC reported United Airlines said it will block agents from booking tickets, and that Amazon prevents agents from buying on its platform.

Amex's Luke Gebb told CNBC: "It just makes sense to watch it, start it in a contained environment, and then keep rolling from there."

Musk's bigger bet: the agent flood
Elon Musk has his own thesis about where this goes. It did not come in response to Wallet.

On Nov. 14 at 12:01 PM ET, in a thread about Starlink bandwidth, Musk replied to a user who had calculated how much global traffic would have to grow for Starlink to carry about half of it. Musk wrote: "Internet traffic will grow by several orders of magnitude, due to super intelligence agents."

That reply had about 220,000 views when we checked at 2:33 AM ET.

It is a claim about capacity, not commerce. But if agents do become a big share of online traffic, they will need ways to pay, and stores will need ways to tell a legitimate agent from a bad bot.

That evening, at 8:13 PM ET, Musk reposted, without comment, a post by user Robin Ebers. Ebers wrote that "Grok Bot is the only one that stuck," and said of ChatGPT Dots: "i’ve literally paused mine due to bugs and constant refusals or annoying prompts to approve."

That is one user's experience, not a test result. The repost is not Musk's own words. And note the last complaint: "annoying prompts to approve." That friction is exactly what OpenAI built Wallet around.

What we don't know
Fees later. CNBC says no cut to start. Nothing says what comes next.
When limits arrive. OpenAI gave no date for pre-approved purchases.
Expansion. No timeline for other plans, other countries or debit cards.
Acceptance. No list of merchants where Wallet reliably completes checkout.
Bugs. No data we found tests Ebers' complaints.
What to watch
The big shift is already in OpenAI's own words: "Over time, we expect users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases."

OpenAI says that would come with "enhanced safeguards."

When that arrives, the user is no longer approving each purchase. They are approving a policy. Watch for:

How limits are set, and who can change them
Whether a disputed charge under a pre-approved rule is treated like any other card dispute
Whether big retailers open the door to agents, or close it
Whether rival agents, including Grok Bot, get wallets of their own
Bottom line
ChatGPT Wallet is cautious by design: a small group of users, every purchase gated by a face or fingerprint, no real card number in the agent's hands, and no OpenAI cut at the start.

The cautious part is the launch. OpenAI has already said where it wants to go: purchases delegated entirely to the agent, within limits you set once.

Musk is betting agents will flood the internet. OpenAI is building the checkout for that world. The fight now is over who sets the rules on spending.
